name: API Gateway
intent: Put one front door in front of many backend services, so that routing, authentication, rate limiting and other shared concerns are handled once instead of in every service.
scenario: A shop has separate user, order and payment services. A mobile app calls all three. Each service team has re-implemented token checks and rate limits slightly differently.
problem: Without a front door, clients must know every service's address, and every service must repeat the same cross-cutting work: authentication, rate limits, logging, TLS, request validation. These copies drift apart, and each internal service is exposed directly to the internet.

howItWorks.title: One entry point for clients
howItWorks.text: Clients call a single host such as api.shop.com. The gateway maps each path (/users, /orders, /pay) to the right internal service, so clients do not know or care how the backend is split, and services can be moved or renamed without client changes.

howItWorks.title: A pipeline of shared checks
howItWorks.text: Every request passes through the same stages: terminate TLS, authenticate the token, apply rate limits, validate the request, then route. Checks run once at the edge, so a rejected request never reaches a service.

howItWorks.title: Translate and combine
howItWorks.text: The gateway can adapt protocols (public REST to internal gRPC), version routes, and sometimes combine several service calls into one response for a screen (a backend-for-frontend). Keep this light: business logic belongs in services.

howItWorks.title: Protect the backends
howItWorks.text: The gateway adds timeouts, retries and circuit breakers per service, can cache safe responses, and sheds load when a service is slow, so one failing service does not hang every client.

howItWorks.title: Make the gateway itself reliable
howItWorks.text: Every request goes through it, so it must be stateless, run as several instances behind a load balancer, and stay fast. Keep its configuration in version control and roll changes out gradually.

pros: Authentication, rate limiting and logging are implemented once
Clients see one stable address and shape, whatever the backend looks like
Internal services are not exposed directly
A natural place for versioning, caching and observability
cons: A single point of failure and a possible bottleneck if poorly run
An extra network hop adds a little latency
A team can turn it into a dumping ground for business logic
Configuration mistakes affect every API at once
whenToUse: Several backend services behind one public API
Shared concerns (auth, limits, logging) that should not be repeated per service
Different clients (mobile, web, partners) needing tailored routes
whenNotToUse: A single service, where a gateway only adds a hop
As a place to put business rules or orchestration that belongs in services
Between internal services that already trust each other and talk through a service mesh
pitfalls: Putting business logic in the gateway until it becomes a bottleneck for every team
Running one gateway instance with no redundancy
Skipping authorization in services because the gateway 'already checked'
Letting backend services stay reachable from the internet, bypassing the gateway

roles.label: Backend service
roles.description: Does the real work behind the gateway.

quiz.question: A shop has separate services for users, orders and payments, and its mobile app calls each directly with its own copy of the login check and rate limiter. The team keeps finding that the three limiters disagree. What is the best change?
options: Copy the best limiter code into all three services, so that every one of them agrees
Give the mobile app a library that enforces the rate limiting on the phone itself
Put a gateway in front that does login and limits once, then routes
Add a fourth service that only stores the shared rate limit settings for the others
quiz.explanation: A gateway applies cross-cutting checks at one entry point. Client-side limits can be bypassed, and sharing settings still leaves three implementations.

quiz.question: An engineer proposes that the gateway should compute order discounts and call the pricing and stock services itself, because that is where all requests pass anyway. What is the best response?
options: Keep the rules in a service, since gateway logic becomes a shared bottleneck
Agree, since the gateway is the only place that already sees all of the requests
Agree, but only if the gateway runs as one single instance, so the results stay consistent
Decline, because a gateway is not able to call more than one backend for each request
quiz.explanation: Gateways may combine calls lightly, but business rules belong in services. A single instance would add a point of failure, and gateways can fan out to several backends.

quiz.question: The gateway authenticates every token and checks the user's role. The orders service trusts that and just returns the order with the id in the URL. A logged-in user changes the id and sees another customer's order. What is the real flaw?
options: The gateway should have cached the validated token for a longer time, to be faster
The orders service skipped its own ownership check on the order
The gateway should also have validated the format of the order id in the URL path
The orders service should be reachable from the internet directly, to share the load better
quiz.explanation: A gateway can verify tokens and roles, but only the service knows who owns order 7. Format validation would not stop a valid id, and exposing the service would make things worse.
